domains.title: Messenger of Frigg
domains.subtitle: Swift Errand-Runner Across Worlds
domains.lead: Gná is one of the Ásynjur, the goddesses of the Norse pantheon, and the special messenger of Frigg. Her horse, Hofvarpnir, runs through air and over sea, carrying her wherever the queen of the gods sends her. She is not a warrior or a mother in the surviving sources; she is speed, service, and the unseen thread that keeps the divine household in motion.

cards.name: Hofvarpnir
cards.desc: Her horse, born of Hófvarpni and Hamskerpir, can gallop through the sky and across the waves.

cards.name: Errands of Frigg
cards.desc: Gná carries the queen's word to every corner of the cosmos, the diplomatic courier of Ásgarðr.

cards.name: The Falling Gná
cards.desc: A farmer once mocked her from a fence; she made the fence-post fall, teaching him to respect a goddess.

cards.name: Swift as Wind
cards.desc: She is the answer Frigg gives when asked which Ásynjur can be trusted to move between worlds without delay.

mythology.lead: Gná's mythology is compact: she appears in Snorri's catalogue of the Ásynjur, where her speed and her horse are her defining traits.

myths.title: The Messenger Goddess
myths.text: In Snorri's list of the Ásynjur, Gná is the one Frigg sends on errands into other worlds. Her horse Hofvarpnir can run through the air and over the sea. The horse's lineage is given: it was born of Hófvarpni and Hamskerpir. Wherever Frigg needs a presence, Gná is the one who arrives.

myths.title: The Fence and the Farmer
myths.text: Snorri adds a single anecdote: once, as Gná rode past, a farmer called out from a fence and asked who she was. She told him to say that she was Gná, sent by Frigg. The farmer replied that the fence was too high for her to leap. Gná then made the fence-post fall, and the fence with it, and rode on. The story is small but memorable: even a minor goddess can undo the fixed world when mocked.

myths.title: Among the Goddesses
myths.text: Gná appears in the þulur and in Snorri's catalogue as one of the fourteen (or more) Ásynjur. She has no husband or children named in the sources; her identity is entirely functional. She is the messenger, and the messenger is defined by the message she carries.

lore.syncretism: Gná has no clear foreign double, but her function — the divine messenger riding a supernatural horse — places her in a common Germanic and Indo-European type. The Vedic Pūṣan and Greek Hermês are wandering messengers with swift horses or sandals; the Irish Manannán rides Aonbharr over sea and land. Within Norse mythology, her closest counterpart is the god Hermóðr, who rides to Hel to bargain for Baldr. Gná is the feminine form of the type: not a psychopomp, but the queen's own courier.
lore.culturalLegacy: Gná remains a minor but beloved figure in modern retellings of Norse myth. Her name is sometimes given to characters who embody swiftness or loyal service, and her horse Hofvarpnir appears in games and fiction as a mount that can run on air. In Heathen practice she is occasionally invoked for matters of communication, travel, and the safe delivery of messages. Restoring Gná preserves the acute accent and long vowel that mark her as one of the Ásynjur rather than a modern abbreviation.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Gná is the goddess of the reliable message. She does not decide what is said; she makes sure it arrives. In a pantheon full of warriors and kings, she is the one who keeps the lines open — the diplomatic pouch, the swift horse, the word that cannot be delayed.

Her one recorded miracle is the falling fence: when a man doubted her passage, the obstacle removed itself. The story is a lesson in the power of divine errand-runners and in the folly of measuring a goddess by her apparent rank. Speed, attention, and faithful delivery are her virtues, and they are rarer than they look.

lore.archaeology: Gná is a purely textual figure. No runestone, image, or place-name is securely hers. Her only witnesses are the manuscripts of Snorri's Prose Edda and the associated þulur name-lists.
